questions.problem:
For the function of two variables 
$f(x,y)={e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},$
the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)=a+b{x}^{2}+c{y}^{2}.
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$
questions.worked_solution:
If the function $f(x,y)$ is twice differentiable at $(x,y)=(0,0),$ then the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈\overset{\text{Linear approximation}}{\overset{⏞}{f(0,0)+{f}_{x}(0,0)\cdot x+{f}_{y}(0,0)\cdot y}} \\  & \,\,+{{\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(0,0)\cdot {x}^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(0,0)\cdot xy+{f}_{yy}(0,0)\cdot {y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial.

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,0) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =2x{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}, & \,{f}_{y}(x,y) & =2y{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\ {f}_{x}(0,0) & =0, & \,{f}_{y}(0,0) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(x,y) & =2(1+2{x}^{2}){e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}, & \,{f}_{xx}(0,0) & =2 \\ {f}_{xy}(x,y) & =4xy{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}, & \,{f}_{xy}(0,0) & =0 \\ {f}_{yy}(x,y) & =2(1+2{y}^{2}){e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}, & \,{f}_{yy}(0,0) & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈1+0\cdot x+0\cdot y+\frac{1}{2}(2\cdot {x}^{2}+2(0)\cdot xy+2\cdot {y}^{2}) \\  & =1+1{x}^{2}+1{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=1+1+1=3.
$$

$$

$$

$$

questions.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defened by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial:

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y)+x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y) & -x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{′}(1,1) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivative, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)-x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y) & x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y) \\ x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y) & -x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y)\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{″}(1,1) & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈0+[\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the sum of the missing expressions is

$$
0+(-1)+(x-1)+(x-1)+2+(x-1)=3x-2.
$$

f(x)≈-1+[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1 \\ z-1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1 \\ z-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1 \\ z-1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, evaluating the polynomial at $x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,2,0) & ≈-1+[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0-1 \\ 2-1 \\ 0-1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}0-1 \\ 2-1 \\ 0-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0-1 \\ 2-1 \\ 0-1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-1+[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-1+(-4)+\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =-5+\frac{1}{2}(-6) \\  & =-8.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Determine the quadratic Taylor polynomial for the function of two variables 
$f(x,y) = \cos(x+y)$
about the point $(0,0).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If the function $f(x,y)$ is twice differentiable at $(x,y) = (0,0),$ then the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈\overset{\text{Linear approximation}}{\overset{⏞}{f(0,0)+{f}_{x}(0,0)\cdot x+{f}_{y}(0,0)\cdot y}} \\  & \,\,+{{\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(0,0)\cdot {x}^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(0,0)\cdot xy+{f}_{yy}(0,0)\cdot {y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial.

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,0) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y), & \,{f}_{y}(x,y) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y) \\ {f}_{x}(0,0) & =0, & \,{f}_{y}(0,0) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(x,y) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x\,+\,y), & \,{f}_{xx}(0,0) & =-1 \\ {f}_{xy}(x,y) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x\,+\,y), & \,{f}_{xy}(0,0) & =-1 \\ {f}_{yy}(x,y) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x\,+\,y), & \,{f}_{yy}(0,0) & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈1+0\cdot x+0\cdot y+\frac{1}{2}((-1)\cdot {x}^{2}+2(-1)\cdot xy+(-1)\cdot {y}^{2}) \\  & =1-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}-xy-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
